passage: The robotics club room at the community centre smelled of solder and samosas. Sunaina had just taken a group photo beside their line-following robot and was already typing a caption for the club page. "Wait," Eshaan said. His cheek was still puffed up from the dentist that morning, and in the photo he looked like he was hiding a golf ball in it. He kept his voice even. "I'm not okay with that one going up. Can you crop me out or take another?" Karan groaned. "Bro, it's funny. Nobody cares." Eshaan's ears went hot, but he didn't laugh along. "I care. It's my face." Sunaina looked from one to the other, then deleted the photo right there and turned the screen so Eshaan could see. "Retake, everyone. Eshaan, stand behind the flag." Karan muttered, but he posed. Afterwards Sunaina said quietly, "Thanks for just saying it. I'd rather know."

qa.q: Why was Eshaan's cheek puffed up?
qa.a: Eshaan's cheek was still puffed up from the dentist that morning.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when Karan called the photo funny?
qa.a: Eshaan felt embarrassed and a bit pressured, his ears going hot, yet steady enough not to laugh along. He may also have been worried about the whole club seeing it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Eshaan named the limit calmly and offered options, crop or retake, and Sunaina deleted it on the spot, so the refusal was respected without a fight. 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Sunaina when Eshaan said no?
qa.a: Sunaina seemed grateful rather than annoyed, saying she'd rather know, so the limit made things between them easier, not harder.

grounding: It shows a teenager setting a calm limit about sharing a photo, one peer respecting it at once, and another's pressure being met with a steady no.

passage:
Monday. At the bus stop Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks. "The lodger at home grabs me when he's drunk. Promise you won't tell. Promise." Shalini hooked his little finger with hers. "Promise."
Wednesday. In science, Mr Iyer lifted his hand to point at the board, and Deepak flinched so hard his pencil box fell. Shalini hardly slept that night. A promise was a promise. But the marks.
Thursday. At lunch Shalini went to the counsellor's room. "I promised not to tell, but I think someone is hurting Deepak." Mrs Rao put her pen down and listened to all of it. "Thank you. You were right to bring this to me. A promise can't cover someone getting hurt." She called Deepak in before the last bell and phoned the school safeguarding lead that same afternoon. At the gate Shalini said, "I broke it because I care." Deepak said nothing, but he didn't walk away.

qa.q: What did Deepak show Shalini at the bus stop?
qa.a: Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling on Wednesday night?
qa.a: Shalini felt torn and worried: loyal to the promise, but frightened for Deepak after the flinch and the marks, which is why she hardly slept.

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao do that helped?
qa.a: Mrs Rao listened fully, thanked Shalini, said a promise can't cover someone getting hurt, saw Deepak before the last bell and phoned the safeguarding lead that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel about the broken promise?
qa.a: Deepak may feel scared or let down at first, which could explain the silence, but not walking away hints at some relief that an adult now knows.

grounding: It shows a teenager first keeping a peer's secret about harm and then telling a trusted adult, who acts the same day, as the caring choice.

passage: The final whistle went at the district sports club, and the scoreboard still read 0–3. Imran yanked off his bib and flung it at the bench. "That's it. I'm quitting. I'm never playing with this team again, I swear." His voice cracked on the last word. A few juniors froze mid-sip. Coach Uma didn't argue. She picked up the bib, folded it and held it out. "You can quit. Just not tonight. Tonight you're too angry to hear yourself. Come to the ground tomorrow after breakfast and tell me then." Imran snatched the bib and stomped to the bus. Next morning he turned up in slippers, hands in his pockets. "I don't want to quit," he mumbled. "I want to stop being played at left back when I'm a striker." Coach Uma nodded slowly. "That, we can talk about."

qa.q: What did the scoreboard read at the final whistle?
qa.a: The scoreboard still read 0–3.

qa.q: What does Imran's cracking voice suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Imran was angry and deeply disappointed, and possibly ashamed of the loss; the vow came from that rush of feeling rather than a settled decision.

qa.q: Why was Coach Uma's 'just not tonight' a wise response?
qa.a: She neither argued nor accepted the vow but gave it a night to settle, and next morning the real wish came out: to play as a striker.

qa.q: How might the juniors who froze have seen the outburst?
qa.a: They may have been startled and unsure whether an older player was really leaving, which shows how a public vow made in anger unsettles others too.

grounding: It shows a teenager swearing to quit in a burst of anger and a coach suggesting a night's wait, after which the real intention comes out.

passage: In the corridors of their Nairobi secondary school, Chen had a new habit: whenever Wanjiru walked by, he suddenly needed to tie a shoelace that was already tied. In chemistry he teased her about her spiky handwriting, then went red to the ears when she laughed. At night he typed long messages and sent only "did u get the homework". Otieno said, "She likes you, obviously. She sat next to you on the bus." Chen wasn't sure. She sat next to everyone. On Friday, by the bike rack, he made himself ask. "I kind of like you. Like, like-like. Do you feel the same, or no?" Wanjiru looked surprised, then kind. "I like you as a friend, Chen. Not that way. Sorry." His face burned. "Okay. Thanks for telling me straight." On Monday he said hi to her normally, and meant it.

qa.q: What did Chen send at night after typing long messages?
qa.a: Chen sent only "did u get the homework".

qa.q: What was Chen feeling each time Wanjiru walked by?
qa.a: Chen was most likely nervous and shy because of a crush, shown by the fake shoelace tying and going red; it could also be plain awkwardness, which is why asking mattered.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Chen asked directly instead of trusting Otieno's guess, and accepted Wanjiru's no politely, so their friendship could carry on.

qa.q: What might Wanjiru have needed when Chen asked?
qa.a: Wanjiru needed room to answer honestly without pressure, and Chen thanking her and greeting her normally on Monday gave her that.

grounding: It shows a first crush coming out as blushing, teasing and avoidance, unclear signals from the other side, and respect meaning asking directly and accepting a no.

passage: Ganga-didi had moved to Bengaluru for her first job in June, and since then she had sent Manoj a meme every single night: cats in hostels, engineers crying, a mango in sunglasses. Manoj, in the family's Indore flat, replied to every one with a single thumbs-up 👍. Nothing else. After two months Ganga called Maa. "Is he angry with me? Just thumbs, like I'm his tuition teacher." Maa laughed and passed the phone over. "Manoj, your didi thinks you hate her memes." Manoj went red. "I don't hate them. The thumbs means got it, I saw, still here. Everyone in my class does that." Then, quieter: "I screenshot all of them. I have a folder called Didi." There was a pause on the line. "You could have just said," Ganga said, her voice wobbly. That night he typed: "👍 and also I miss you."

qa.q: Where did Ganga move for her first job?
qa.a: Ganga moved to Bengaluru for her first job in June.

qa.q: What does Manoj's folder called Didi suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Manoj felt real affection and missed Ganga; the bare thumbs-up was his class's way of saying 'I saw', not coldness, even though it read as distant.

qa.q: What could Ganga have done sooner?
qa.a: Ganga could have asked Manoj directly what the thumbs-up meant instead of worrying for two months and checking through Maa.

qa.q: How did the thumbs-up look from Ganga's side?
qa.a: To Ganga it looked flat, like a reply to a tuition teacher, so she worried Manoj was angry with her.

grounding: It shows a teenager's affection hidden inside a bare digital reaction whose meaning differs between groups, and a direct question clearing it up.

passage:
Sunday night
Irfan finally posted the kathak video, the one he's been practising in the society parking lot for weeks. I tapped the heart in about half a second, same as the 63 other people. Then I felt oddly guilty, like I'd clapped from the back of a hall. A heart costs nothing. I'd watched him fall on that spin at least ten times in the parking lot. So I wrote to him separately: "The spin at 0:41!!! You nailed the one you kept falling on. And your hands at the end looked just like your teacher's. So proud of you 😊" Took me ten minutes to send it, because it felt like too much. He replied in two: "Pooja. I've read this four times. Everyone else just liked it." Then a voice note of him doing a tiny victory thump on the floor. Hearts are nice. Words are better. Noting that down.

qa.q: At what point in the video was the spin?
qa.a: The spin Irfan nailed was at 0:41.

qa.q: Why did Pooja feel guilty after tapping the heart?
qa.a: The heart felt too easy, like clapping from the back of a hall, after watching Irfan fall on that spin so many times. There was also some nervousness, since the real message took ten minutes to send.

qa.q: What made Pooja's message land better than the like?
qa.a: It was specific, naming the spin at 0:41 and the hands at the end, and showed Pooja had really watched the practice, which a quick heart can't show. 😊

qa.q: How did the messages look to Irfan?
qa.a: Irfan read Pooja's message four times because everyone else just liked the video, so the specific words meant more than the count of hearts.

grounding: It shows a teenager expressing admiration first with a quick like and then with a specific personal message that means much more.

passage: At Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall, Jomon Sir held up a sheet and announced, "The best essay in the whole of class ten came from Usha Verma. Come up, Usha." Two hundred heads turned. Usha's cheeks went pink and the corners of her mouth kept twitching upward, but she walked to the stage like it was a punishment, hands balled into her sleeves. "Sir must have mixed up the pages," she said into the mic. Everyone laughed. She laughed too, then stared at her shoes until she could leave. Later, in the corridor, Farah said, "You looked like you wanted to vanish. Did you hate it?" Usha shook her head. "I loved it. I just hated everyone looking." That afternoon Jomon Sir stopped by her desk and said quietly, "Your ending made me think for a long time." Usha didn't joke that time. She said, "Thank you, Sir," and smiled properly.

qa.q: Where did Jomon Sir praise the essay?
qa.a: He praised it at Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she walked to the stage?
qa.a: Usha felt pleased but embarrassed by the attention, with a twitching smile and balled hands; the joke deflected the exposure rather than showing dislike of the praise.

qa.q: Which kind of praise suited Usha better, and why?
qa.a: The quiet word at her desk suited her better because it was specific and private, so she could simply enjoy it without everyone looking.

qa.q: How did Farah read Usha's behaviour on stage?
qa.a: Farah thought Usha looked like she wanted to vanish and wondered if she hated it, which shows how squirming at praise can be misread.

grounding: It shows a teenager looking pleased yet squirming and joking when praised in front of peers, and a quiet private word suiting her better.

passage: You're asking whether that senior's compliments are real, Swati? Then let your Thomas Uncle tell you about 1989. I was in class ten at a boys' school in Bangalore, and a senior, Victor, started calling me "the best spinner in the city". Every day. Loudly. I floated for a week. Then one evening he said, "Such a genius bowler can surely write my history project, no?" And I did it, twice, before it clicked. Meanwhile our games teacher, Mr Pinto, hardly ever praised me. But when he did, it was small and exact: "Your wrist was straighter today, keep that." He said the same thing whether others were listening or not, and he never asked me for anything. I'm not saying Victor was a crook. Maybe he half meant it; I'll never know. But I learned to listen for the specific, the steady, and the favour that follows. Now pass me that tea before it goes cold.

qa.q: What did Victor call Thomas every day?
qa.a: Victor called Thomas "the best spinner in the city".

qa.q: What was young Thomas feeling during that first week of praise?
qa.a: Thomas was flattered and happy, floating for a week; after writing the project twice he likely felt foolish and used, though Victor may have half meant it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story would you have made differently, and why?
qa.a: Young Thomas could have paused when the favour arrived right after the compliments; noticing that the praise came with a request would have saved him writing the project twice.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto have seen his own small, exact comments?
qa.a: Mr Pinto likely saw them as honest coaching, saying the same thing whether others were listening or not, with nothing wanted in return.

grounding: It shows an elder's memory of strategic praise versus specific, consistent praise with no request attached, while admitting motives can't be confirmed from words alone.

subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
At 12:50 Dhruv knocked and stood in the doorway for a long moment before sitting. He kept twisting his watch strap. He said Jomon had messaged him last night: "don't tell anyone, but sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." Dhruv said he had promised to keep it secret and felt like a traitor for coming. I told him he had done exactly the right thing, that this was too big for one friend to hold, and that he was not in trouble, and neither was Jomon. I asked him to wait in my room while I fetched Jomon from the lab myself. I spoke with Jomon until 2:30; his mother came to school at 3 and we made a safety plan together. Before Dhruv left, I said he could check in with me tomorrow. He asked, "Will Jomon hate me?" I said Jomon might be upset for a while, and that caring sometimes feels like that.

qa.q: What time did Dhruv knock?
qa.a: Dhruv knocked at 12:50.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he twisted his watch strap?
qa.a: Dhruv felt anxious and guilty, torn between the promise and fear for Jomon; the long pause in the doorway also suggests he feared being blamed.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do straight away that helped?
qa.a: The counsellor told Dhruv he had done the right thing, fetched Jomon at once, talked with Jomon until 2:30, and brought in Jomon's mother that afternoon to make a safety plan.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about Dhruv telling?
qa.a: Jomon might feel upset or betrayed at first, but being met straight away by the counsellor and a parent may also bring relief at not carrying it alone.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising that a friend's hopeless message is too big to hold alone and telling a trusted adult despite being asked for secrecy.

passage: Last month Keerthana found out she hadn't made the state volleyball squad, and I said exactly the wrong thing first. We were sitting on the steps behind the court and she was ripping a leaf into tiny strips. I said, "Hey, it's not a big deal, there's always next year. You could work on your serve." She went completely still. "Thanks, Lalit. Very helpful," she said, flat as a wall, and got up. I felt stupid. That night I didn't send tips. I wrote: "Sorry about earlier. I know how much you wanted this. I'm not going to fix it. I'm just around if you want to rant." She called twenty minutes later and talked for almost an hour, mostly about her coach and how unfair the trial felt. I said maybe ten sentences. At the end she said, "That helped." I still don't know what I said. I think that was the point.

qa.q: Where were they sitting when Lalit said the wrong thing?
qa.a: They were sitting on the steps behind the court.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel after Keerthana walked away?
qa.a: Lalit felt stupid and probably guilty for shrinking the disappointment, which is why the night message apologised and offered listening instead of tips.

qa.q: What changed between the first reply and the night message?
qa.a: Lalit stopped fixing and minimising, named how much Keerthana wanted it, apologised and offered to listen, which let her talk for almost an hour.

qa.q: What was it like for Keerthana to hear 'it's not a big deal'?
qa.a: It made Keerthana feel her disappointment was brushed aside, so she went still, answered flatly and left.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning that minimising and quick fixes feel dismissive, while listening and a supportive message help someone who is hurting.
